sections.body:
Our office is in Gilbert, and we have been roofing in the Valley since 1993. Most of our jobs are in the East Valley, where we can reach a home quickly and come back easily for follow-up work. We also take jobs across the wider Phoenix area.

We have detailed pages for our three busiest cities. Each one covers the age of local homes, common roof types, monsoon and heat concerns, and how permits and HOA approval usually work there.
bullets: Mesa: see roofing in Mesa, AZ
Chandler: see roofing in Chandler, AZ
Gilbert: see roofing in Gilbert, AZ
Also served: Queen Creek, San Tan Valley, Tempe, Phoenix, Scottsdale, Apache Junction, Ahwatukee, Glendale and Peoria

sections.body:
Mesa is the oldest and largest of the three. It was founded in 1878, and its population grew from 63,049 in 1970 to 288,091 in 1990. That means many Mesa neighborhoods have roofs that are 30 years old or more, plus a large set of 55+ communities with older shingle and low-slope roofs. East Mesa also has brand-new master-planned communities such as Eastmark.

Chandler grew fastest in the 1980s and 1990s, from 29,673 residents in 1980 to 176,581 in 2000. Much of the city is concrete tile on homes from that era, now reaching the age when the underlayment beneath the tile needs attention.

Gilbert is the youngest. It had 5,717 residents in 1980 and 267,918 in 2020. Most homes are tile-roofed production homes from the mid-1980s on, and nearly every neighborhood has an HOA.

sections.h2: Common roof types in the East Valley
sections.body: Concrete tile on a sloped roof is the most common roof we see on East Valley homes, especially on houses built from the late 1980s on. Older homes and many 55+ communities often have asphalt shingles, and a lot of homes in every era have a flat or low-slope section over a patio, addition or Territorial-style roofline.
bullets: Tile roofs (concrete and clay): the tile lasts a long time, but the underlayment beneath it wears out and eventually needs a lift and relay
Asphalt shingles: common on older homes and many retirement communities; heat and UV shorten their life
Spray foam roofs: common on flat sections and Territorial-style homes; the protective coating needs periodic recoating
Flat roofs and elastomeric coatings: patio covers, additions and commercial buildings

sections.body:
Arizona's monsoon season officially runs June 15–September 30. Storms bring sudden wind, dust and short bursts of heavy rain, and that is when we see the most broken tiles, lifted shingles and leaks at flashing. Average July highs in Mesa, Chandler and Gilbert are all around 106°F, and that heat, along with strong UV, wears down shingles, foam coatings and exposed underlayment year-round.

The best time to find problems is before the season starts. A spring roof inspection catches slipped tiles, cracked flashing and worn coatings while they are still small repairs. After a big storm, check your ceilings and yard for signs of damage and see our damaged roof page.

Re-roofing in the Valley is regulated by each city's building department, and the rules depend on the city and the scope of the job. Some communities with East Valley mailing addresses, such as Sun Lakes and several Mesa county islands, are unincorporated, so permitting goes through Maricopa County instead. We confirm what is required for your address before work starts.

If your home is in an HOA, you usually need architectural approval before changing roof color, tile profile or material. We can give you the product details your HOA asks for. Some condo and townhome associations handle roof replacement themselves, so check your CC&Rs first.

We handle residential and commercial roofing on tile, shingle, foam, flat and coated roofs. Financing is available, and you can ask about it during your estimate. For cost questions, start with our roofing cost guide; every roof is different, so a real number comes from an inspection.

sections.body:
Mesa was founded in 1878 and incorporated in 1883. It counted 504,258 residents in the 2020 census, making it the third-largest city in Arizona. Most of that growth came fast: the population went from 63,049 in 1970 to 152,453 in 1980, 288,091 in 1990 and 396,375 in 2000.

That history shapes the roofing work here. A large share of Mesa's neighborhoods went up in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, so many roofs are now 25 to 50 years old. On those homes we see a lot of tile underlayment replacement, shingle re-roofs and worn flat sections. In southeast Mesa, communities such as Eastmark (opened in 2013) and Cadence at Gateway (first phase 2018) are still young, and the work there is mostly storm repairs and small fixes.

sections.h2: Common roof types by era of homes
sections.body: Roof type in Mesa tracks closely with when a neighborhood was built. Here is what we typically find, with examples drawn from public listing records:
bullets: 1950s–1970s homes and early retirement communities: composition shingles and low-slope sections. Listings in Mesa Grande (1969), Sunland Village (built 1974–1984) and Dreamland Villa (opened 1959) show composition roofs.

1970s–1980s master-planned communities: Dobson Ranch, one of Mesa's oldest master-planned communities, was built between 1973 and 1999. Homes of this era usually have shingle or tile pitched roofs, often with a flat patio section.
Late 1980s–1990s subdivisions: concrete tile becomes standard. Listings in Alta Mesa (1988), Red Mountain Ranch (1994), Superstition Springs (1995) and Augusta Ranch (1999) show concrete tile.
Foothill and custom homes: Las Sendas homes from the late 1990s on use concrete tile, while some Territorial-style custom homes in the northeast foothills have flat foam roofs.
2010s to today: concrete tile on production homes in Eastmark, Cadence at Gateway and Mountain Bridge.

sections.h2: What older tile roofs in Mesa need
sections.body:
Concrete tile can outlast the house, but it is not the waterproof layer. The underlayment beneath the tile does that job, and it dries out and cracks with age and heat. On Mesa homes from the 1990s or earlier, the original underlayment is often at or past the end of its life even when the tile looks fine from the street.

The fix is usually a tile underlayment replacement, also called a re-felt or lift and relay: we remove the tile, install new underlayment and flashing, and reset the good tile. It costs less than a full replacement and keeps the look your HOA approved. See our roofing cost guide for how pricing works.

Mesa summers are long and hot. At the East Mesa weather station, the average high is 104.1°F in June, 105.9°F in July and 104.6°F in August, and the record is 121°F. That heat and the strong UV break down shingles, foam coatings and any underlayment exposed at edges and valleys.

Mesa averages about 10.76 inches of rain a year, and July, August and September are the wettest months. That rain mostly arrives in monsoon storms between June 15 and September 30, often with high wind and blowing debris. One storm can crack tiles, lift shingles and push water past tired flashing.

sections.body:
Re-roofing inside Mesa city limits is regulated by the City of Mesa's building department. Requirements depend on the scope of the work, so we confirm what your address needs before the job starts and handle any permit the work requires.

Not every Mesa address is in the city. Leisure World and Dreamland Villa are unincorporated Maricopa County islands surrounded by Mesa, so building permits there go through the county.

Many Mesa neighborhoods also have HOA rules. Las Sendas, for example, has an architectural review process and published CC&Rs, so plan for approval before changing tile color or profile. In some condo associations, such as certain sections of Sunland Village East, roof replacement is included in the HOA fee and the association handles it. Check your CC&Rs before you schedule work.
We work on homes and commercial buildings across Mesa, on tile, shingle, foam, flat and coated roofs. Financing is available; ask about it during your estimate.

What roof types are most common in Mesa?

Concrete tile is the most common on homes built from the late 1980s on. Older homes and many 55+ communities have composition shingles, and flat foam or coated sections are common on patios, additions and Territorial-style homes.
My Mesa home was built in the 1980s or 1990s. Does it need a new roof?

Not necessarily. If it has concrete tile, the tile may still be sound, but the original underlayment beneath it is likely worn out. A tile underlayment replacement often solves the problem for less than a full re-roof. An inspection will tell you which you need.
What is a lift and relay?

A lift and relay, or re-felt, means removing the roof tile, installing new underlayment and flashing, and reinstalling the existing tile. Broken pieces are replaced with matching tile. It renews the waterproof layer without buying all new tile.
Do I need a permit to re-roof in Mesa?

When is monsoon season in Mesa?
Monsoon season officially runs June 15–September 30. July, August and September are Mesa's wettest months, and storms often bring strong wind and blowing debris along with rain.

Take photos of any damage you can see safely from the ground, and check ceilings for new stains. Then call us at 602-548-3770 during office hours. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.
Do you repair foam roofs in Mesa?
Yes. We repair spray foam roofs and recoat them. Foam depends on its top coating to block UV, so keeping that coating in good shape is the most important maintenance.

sections.body:
Chandler started as a ranch. Alexander J. Chandler, the first veterinary surgeon in the Arizona Territory, settled here in 1891, the town-site office opened in 1912, and the town was incorporated in 1920. For decades it stayed small: Chandler had 29,673 residents in 1980.

Then it boomed. By 2000 the population was 176,581, nearly six times the 1980 count, and the 2020 census counted 275,987. Intel, the city's largest employer with 12,000 workers, anchors a tech economy that drove much of that growth.

For roofing, that means a large share of Chandler's homes date from the late 1980s through the mid-2000s. Most have concrete tile, and many are now 20 to 35 years old. The tile often still looks good, but the underlayment beneath it is wearing out, so tile underlayment replacement is one of the most common jobs we do here.

sections.h2: Common roof types by era of homes
sections.body: Here is what we usually find in Chandler, with examples drawn from public listing records:
bullets: Late 1980s homes in north and west Chandler: a mix of shingle and tile. A 1987 home in Twelve Oaks near the Intel campus has composition shingles, while a 1987 home in Andersen Springs has tile.
1990s master-planned communities: concrete tile is standard. Ocotillo, with homes mostly from the 1990s and 2000s, and The Provinces, Clemente Ranch and Fox Crossing all show tile on listings.
2000s south Chandler: concrete tile on communities such as Fulton Ranch (begun 2005), Sun Groves, Cooper Commons and Valencia.
Custom and estate homes: tile with flat sections. Listings in Whitewing at Krueger show a foam roof on one home and tile with hot-mopped flat sections on another.
55+ communities: Springfield (built 1996–2000) and Solera (2001–2005) have tile. Older Sun Lakes homes include foam and built-up flat roofs.

sections.h2: Why tile underlayment matters in Chandler
sections.body:
On a tile roof, the underlayment is the real waterproof layer. The tile shields it from sun and sheds most of the water, but heat slowly dries the underlayment out until it cracks and lets water through, usually at valleys, around penetrations and along the lower edges of the roof.

Since so many Chandler homes were built in the same 15–20 years, whole neighborhoods tend to reach this point together. A lift and relay replaces the underlayment and flashing and reuses the sound tile. It usually costs less than a full re-roof and keeps your home's original look. Our roofing cost guide explains how pricing works.

Chandler's average July high is 106°F, and the record is 119°F. The city averages about 9.20 inches of rain a year. Much of that falls during monsoon season, June 15–September 30, when storms bring strong wind, dust and short, heavy downpours.

Heat and UV do slow damage all year: shingles lose granules, foam coatings wear thin and exposed underlayment breaks down. Monsoon storms do fast damage: cracked and slipped tile, lifted shingles, debris in valleys and water forced past old flashing.

sections.h2: Roof age in Ocotillo depends on the neighborhood
sections.body:
Ocotillo isn't one subdivision. It's a master-planned community of about 40 separate neighborhoods, and they weren't all built at once. Most homes went up in the 1990s and 2000s, building continued into the 2010s, and a few homes were completed in the 2020s.

That spread matters for your roof. A home in the Estates at Ocotillo built in 1996 has a roof that's roughly 30 years old, while the Villas at Villa Del Lago, which Standard Pacific Homes opened in 2015, are only about a decade in. Two homes a mile apart can need completely different work, so we begin every Ocotillo visit by confirming when the house was built and whether the roof has ever been redone.

sections.h2: What the original 1990s roofs usually need now
sections.body:
Pitched roofs from that era in the Chandler area were commonly finished with concrete tile over felt underlayment. The tile can last for decades, but felt underlayment under the Arizona sun usually wears out in about 20–25 years. For any roof in Ocotillo's earliest neighborhoods that is still original, that window has already closed.

When underlayment fails, water that slips past the tile no longer drains off cleanly. Early signs are easy to miss: a faint ceiling stain near an outside wall, a musty attic, or dark spots on the roof deck. The usual fix is a tile underlayment replacement, where we lift the tile, install new underlayment and flashing, and relay the sound tile.

Ocotillo mixes detached houses with townhomes, patio homes and condos. On attached homes, one roof often runs across several units, so a leak above your neighbor's garage can be the same problem that's staining your ceiling.

Who pays for and schedules roof work on attached homes varies by association, and we don't have those rules for each Ocotillo neighborhood. Check your own HOA documents first. If the roof is your responsibility, we can inspect it and explain what we find in a way you can share with the neighbors who share it.

The community is built around interconnected man-made lakes filled with reclaimed water from a City of Chandler treatment plant, plus the 27-hole Ocotillo Golf Club, which Ted Robinson designed in 1986. Plenty of homes back onto water or fairways.

Homes along a golf course can collect cracked or chipped tiles from stray balls. A single broken tile seems minor, but it exposes the underlayment beneath it to direct sun and rain. If you hear a thump on the roof or spot tile fragments in the yard, have the area checked before monsoon season.

Arizona's monsoon season runs June 15–September 30, and the strongest storms bring wind gusts, sideways rain and blowing debris. On tile roofs, the common damage is slipped or broken tiles along ridges and edges, and lifted flashing around walls and vents. Our roof inspections page explains what a post-storm check covers.
bullets: Walk the yard after a big storm and look for tile pieces on the ground.
Check ceilings and the tops of exterior walls for new stains.
Clear leaves and debris from valleys and roof-to-wall corners in late spring.
Schedule an inspection if anything looks out of place rather than waiting for a leak.

sections.h2: Planning roof work in a gated section
sections.body: Some Ocotillo neighborhoods are gated and some are open. If yours is gated, share the gate code or access instructions when you book so our crew isn't stuck at the entrance. For a replacement or any change to the roof's look, most master-planned HOAs require architectural approval before work starts; ask your association what it needs and we'll provide product details for the request.

Do the oldest Ocotillo homes need a new roof?

Not always. If the tile is in good shape, replacing the worn underlayment and relaying the existing tile is often the right repair. An inspection tells you whether that will work or whether a full replacement makes more sense.

That depends on your association's rules, which vary. Check your HOA documents to see whether the roof is maintained by the association or by the owner before scheduling work.
Can golf balls damage a tile roof?
Yes. A direct hit can crack or chip a concrete tile, which leaves the underlayment exposed. Homes along the Ocotillo Golf Club fairways should have broken tiles replaced promptly.

Most master-planned communities require architectural approval for changes to a roof's appearance. Ask your HOA what it needs; we can supply tile color and product details for your application.
What should I check after a monsoon storm?
Look for tile pieces in the yard, displaced ridge tiles, and new ceiling stains. If you see any of those, schedule an inspection before the next storm.
Will your crew be able to get into a gated Ocotillo neighborhood?
Yes, as long as we have access. Give us the gate code or instructions when you schedule and we'll pass them to the crew.

Call us at 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

Every roof is different, so the price depends on size, pitch and the condition of the tile. Our Roofing Cost Guide in the Resources section explains the main cost factors, and we'll give you a written estimate after we see the roof.

A roof that's maintained well during these years tends to give you more time before any major work.

sections.h2: The repairs we expect to see on 10- to 20-year-old tile
sections.body: Mid-life tile roofs rarely fail all at once. Problems tend to start at the details, and catching them early keeps them small.
bullets: Cracked or slipped tiles from foot traffic, wind or falling branches
Flashing that has pulled away at roof-to-wall joints, chimneys or skylights

sections.h2: Why a mid-life inspection pays off here
sections.body:
An inspection on a roof this age is less about finding a disaster and more about knowing where you stand. We check the tile, the flashing and the penetrations, and where we can safely do so, look at the underlayment at a few spots. You get a clear picture of what's fine, what needs attention now and what to plan for in the next several years.

That kind of timeline is useful if you're budgeting, selling, or simply want to avoid surprises. Learn more about what we look at on our roof inspections page.

Fulton Ranch is built around a 28-acre system of lakes, streams and waterfalls, and many homes sit along greenbelts and open water with mature landscaping nearby. During monsoon season, June 15–September 30, strong gusts can lift edge tiles and drop palm fronds and branches onto roofs.

After a storm, look for tile on the ground, debris collected in valleys, and any new stains inside. Small storm damage is a straightforward storm damage repair when it's handled before the next round of rain.

Many Fulton Ranch sub-neighborhoods are gated, including areas such as Crescent Falls, Serenity Shores and The Island, a section of large custom homes. If your street is behind a gate, include the access details when you book.

The community has an HOA, and like most master-planned associations it's likely to review visible changes such as a new tile color or profile. Repairs that match the existing roof usually don't change its look, but check with your HOA before any larger project.

The Island's large custom homes don't follow a single builder plan, so their roofs can have more hips, valleys and roof-to-wall transitions than a typical production home. Every one of those joints is a spot where flashing has to do its job, which makes careful inspection more important on complex roofs.

sections.body:

In the attic, look for dark spots on the underside of the roof deck or daylight around penetrations.

Don't wait for a second storm. Water that sits on decking can cause rot that turns a re-felt into a bigger job.

sections.h2: How we evaluate a 23-year-old tile roof
sections.body:
On a roof this age, we're answering one main question: how much life does the underlayment have left? We check tile for cracks and slipping, look at flashing at walls and valleys, inspect pipe boots and vents, and lift tiles in a few places to see the underlayment directly.

From there, the recommendation is usually one of three things: small repairs now, a lift and relay soon, or a full replacement if the tile itself is in poor shape. Learn more about our roof inspections.

sections.h2: Easy things owners can watch for

Water marks on the underside of the roof deck in the attic
Tiles that look out of line from the street
Leaves and debris piling up in valleys
sections.body: You don't need to climb a ladder to keep tabs on your roof. Most early warnings are visible from the ground or the attic hatch.

sections.h2: Heat, UV and the south-facing slope
sections.body: In Chandler, long summers of triple-digit heat and intense UV are what age underlayment. If we find a problem on one side, we'll check whether the opposite slopes are in better shape, which can affect what we recommend.

sections.h2: Shingle roofs in the Arizona sun
sections.body:
Asphalt shingles generally don't last as long as tile in the Valley. Intense UV and summer heat dry out the asphalt, granules wash off, and shingles curl, crack or blow off in monsoon winds. An original 1980s shingle roof would be far past its expected life, so a shingle roof on a Twelve Oaks home today has most likely been replaced at some point, though we can't say when for any particular house.

If your shingle roof is showing its age, look for:
bullets: Curled, cupped or cracked shingles
Bare spots where granules have worn away
Granules collecting in gutters or at downspouts
Missing shingles after a windy storm
Soft spots when walking near the edges, which can mean damaged decking

sections.h2: Replacing shingles: same material or switch?
sections.body:
When a shingle roof wears out, you can replace it with new asphalt shingles or consider switching to tile. Shingles cost less up front. Tile is heavier and lasts longer, but a house originally framed for shingles may need an engineering review before carrying tile weight.

Any change in roofing material would also likely need HOA approval. We can walk through the trade-offs with you during an estimate, and our roof types page compares the options.

sections.h2: If your Twelve Oaks home has tile
sections.body: If your home has a tile roof, the main concern at this age is the underlayment. Felt typically lasts about 20–25 years under tile in Arizona, so an original underlayment from the late 1980s would be long overdue. If it was replaced at some point, ask when. A lift and relay replaces the underlayment and reuses sound tile; see our tile roofs page.

Twelve Oaks is made up of smaller single-family homes. Smaller footprints often mean simpler roof shapes with fewer valleys and transitions, which can make repairs and replacements more straightforward. We'll still inspect the whole roof, including flashing at walls and any patio covers, before recommending anything.

The Twelve Oaks HOA includes grounds maintenance. That doesn't tell us whether the association handles roofs, so check your HOA documents to confirm who is responsible for roof repairs and replacement before scheduling work. If a project changes the roof's look, ask about approval too.

sections.h2: What 30-plus years does to a tile roof
sections.body:
Concrete tile itself can last a very long time, but the felt underlayment beneath it is the part that keeps water out, and in Arizona heat felt often lasts around 20–25 years. Homes built in Warner Ranch between 1986 and 1994 are now well past that window if they still have their original underlayment.

Aging felt turns brittle, cracks at the laps and starts to tear around vents and valleys. From the street the roof can look fine while the layer underneath has stopped doing its job.
bullets: Water stains on ceilings near exterior walls or around vent pipes
Slipped or cracked tiles that expose the underlayment to sun
Granules or felt fragments collecting in gutters and at downspouts
Attic sheathing that looks dark or soft after a monsoon storm

sections.body:
For many Warner Ranch homes the answer is a tile underlayment replacement, sometimes called a re-felt or lift and relay. We remove the tile, replace the underlayment and flashings, then reinstall the good tiles and swap in matching ones for any that are broken.

A full roof replacement makes more sense when the decking is damaged, when too many tiles are broken to match, or when an owner wants a new look. We explain both options during the estimate and let you decide.

sections.h2: Foam and flat sections on some Warner Ranch homes
sections.body:
At least one Warner Ranch Village listing shows a home with both tile and foam roofing. Low-slope areas over patios, additions or rear rooms are common on homes of this era, and they age differently from the tile.

Spray foam needs a fresh protective coating every several years to block UV. If the coating wears through, the foam underneath starts to erode. We handle foam roof recoats and flat roof repairs alongside tile work, so one visit can cover the whole house.

Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30, and its wind gusts are hard on older tile. A tile that was already loose can lift, slide or break, and wind-driven rain finds any gap in tired underlayment.

After a strong storm, walk the yard and look for broken tile pieces, then check ceilings for new stains over the next few days. If you see damage, our storm damage repair team can document it and make repairs.

A like-for-like re-felt that reuses your existing tile usually changes nothing visible, which tends to make approval simple. We can provide product details for your application.

sections.h2: Why late-1990s tile roofs need attention now
sections.body:
Concrete tile sheds most of the rain, but the felt underlayment below it does the real waterproofing. In the Phoenix area, that felt commonly lasts about 20–25 years before heat makes it brittle.

Ashley Park homes finished in 1997–1999 have crossed that line. Many owners won't see a problem until a heavy storm pushes water through, so a planned inspection now usually costs less than an emergency repair later.

sections.h2: What we look at during an Ashley Park inspection
sections.body: A roof inspection on a Fulton home of this age focuses on the places where water gets in first.
bullets: Valleys, where debris collects and the underlayment wears fastest
Pipe and vent flashings, which often crack or lose their seal
Ridge and hip tiles, checking that mortar or fasteners still hold
Broken, slipped or missing field tiles
Felt exposed at eaves and edges, where sun damage shows first
Attic signs such as stains, daylight or damp insulation

sections.h2: Repair now or plan a re-felt
sections.body:
If the underlayment is still sound in most areas, a targeted roof repair can fix a leak and buy time. We replace broken tiles, reseal flashings and patch the affected section.

When the felt is failing across the roof, a full tile underlayment replacement is the longer-lasting fix. We remove the tile, install new underlayment and flashing, and reset the tile. Because the look of the roof doesn't change, it fits well in an established HOA neighborhood like this one.

sections.h2: Close to downtown, exposed to the same storms
sections.body:
Ashley Park's location near Downtown Chandler and the Loop 202 is convenient, but it doesn't shield homes from monsoon weather. From June 15 to September 30, gusty storms can lift loose tile and drive rain sideways under it.

Trees on mature lots also drop leaves and branches into valleys, which can hold water against the underlayment. Clearing valleys and gutters before monsoon season is an easy way to lower the risk.

We don't have Ashley Park's specific roofing guidelines, but most Arizona HOAs require architectural review for changes to roof color or material. A re-felt that reuses your current tile usually doesn't change the exterior, though it's still wise to check with management first.

If you're switching tile profile or color during a replacement, ask the HOA for its approved list before you choose. We can supply product specs for the application.

If your roof is still original, now is a good time to plan rather than wait for a leak. Planned work lets you choose timing, compare options and budget, instead of reacting during monsoon season.

sections.h2: Choosing between repair, re-felt and replacement
sections.body: We start with an inspection and photos, then recommend the smallest fix that will actually solve the problem.
bullets: Repair: for a single leak, a cracked flashing or a few broken tiles when the felt elsewhere is still sound
Re-felt (lift and relay): new underlayment and flashings with your existing tile reinstalled, the most common choice for 1998 tile roofs
Full replacement: new tile and underlayment when decking is damaged or tile is too broken to reuse

sections.h2: How heat wears down a Chandler roof
sections.body:
Summer roof surfaces in Chandler get far hotter than the air temperature. Day after day, that heat dries out the oils in felt underlayment, which is why it cracks and tears long before the tile wears out.

UV also breaks down sealants around vents and pipe boots. On a 1998 roof, those seals have likely been through several cycles of hardening and cracking, and they are a common source of small, slow leaks we find in homes of this age.

Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30. Strong outflow winds can loosen tile, and the heavy rain that follows tests every weak spot in the underlayment.

Before the season starts, clear gutters and valleys and look from the ground for tiles out of line. After a big storm, check for debris on the roof and new ceiling stains. Our storm damage team can inspect and repair what the wind left behind.

Dobson Place is an HOA subdivision with more than one parcel, and one listing names Standard Pacific as the builder of Parcel 2. We don't have the HOA's roof rules on file, so check your CC&Rs or ask management before changing tile color or profile.

A re-felt that reuses your tile usually leaves the outside looking the same. That said, many associations still like to be told about major roof work, so a quick call to management is worth it.

It sits near the base of the San Tan Mountains and is not part of the City of Chandler. Its old 85227 ZIP code was retired, and addresses there now use Queen Creek.

Robson bought the farmland in 1972. Early sales were lots and mobile homes, single-family homes began in 1976, and the community sold out around 2005–2006. It's organized into five neighborhoods: Sun Lakes Country Club, Cottonwood, Palo Verde, Ironwood and Oakwood, each with its own golf course and amenity center.

Sources disagree on the total number of homes, so we won't quote one. What matters for your roof is your home's age and style, which can vary a lot from one street to the next.

sections.h2: Foam and built-up roofs in older sections
sections.body: Listings show a 1981 Sun Lakes home with a foam roof and a 1986 Cottonwood home with a built-up flat roof. Low-slope roofs like these were common in the community's early decades, and they need different care than tile.
bullets: Foam roofs need their protective coating renewed every several years; worn coating lets UV erode the foam
Built-up (tar and gravel or hot-mop) roofs can blister and crack, especially around edges and drains
Ponding water on any flat roof speeds up wear and should be corrected
Elastomeric coatings can extend the life of some flat roofs that are still sound

sections.h2: Our services for Sun Lakes homes
sections.body:
For low-slope roofs we handle spray foam repair and recoats, elastomeric coatings and flat roof repair and replacement. For tile homes built in later phases, we do repairs, underlayment replacement and full re-roofs.

We start every job with an inspection, explain your options in plain terms, and recommend the least invasive fix that will actually last.

Cottonwood and Palo Verde share one HOA, and Ironwood and Oakwood fall under the IronOaks association. Palo Verde, Ironwood and Oakwood are gated, so let us know gate procedures when you call. Sun Lakes Country Club and Cottonwood aren't gated.

Many Sun Lakes residents like a family member to weigh in on roof decisions. We're happy to meet with both of you, and we share photos so relatives who live farther away can see the condition of the roof for themselves.

Summer storms arrive with monsoon season, June 15–September 30. Spring and fall are the most comfortable times for a check-up, and catching a worn foam coating before summer can prevent a much larger repair.

sections.h2: Mid-life tile roofs: what to expect
sections.body:
Old Stone Ranch was built in phases, with Phase 1 homes from around 2006 and Phase 3 from around 2010. That puts most roofs at 15–20 years old.

Felt underlayment under tile typically lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, so these roofs aren't usually due for a full re-felt yet. This is the stage where regular inspections and small repairs keep the roof healthy and help you plan ahead instead of being surprised.
A little attention at this age goes a long way.
bullets: Replace cracked or slipped tiles before sun reaches the underlayment
Reseal pipe boots and vent flashings as sealant ages
Clear valleys and gutters, especially under mature trees
Check ridge and hip tiles for loose fasteners or mortar
Look in the attic once a year for stains after storms

sections.body:
Because Old Stone Ranch was built over several years, two homes on nearby streets can have roofs four or five years apart in age. A 2006 Phase 1 roof is closer to the typical underlayment lifespan than a 2010 Phase 3 roof.

When you compare your roof with a neighbor's, check the build year first. An inspection gives you a clear picture of where your particular roof stands, and our roof inspections include photos so you can see it for yourself.

Old Stone Ranch is known for its community lakes, parks and tree-lined streets. Trees are great for shade, but leaves and seed pods collect in roof valleys and gutters, where they hold moisture and block drainage.

Clearing debris before monsoon season keeps rainwater moving off the roof. If branches overhang your roof, trimming them back also reduces scuffing and broken tiles when the wind picks up.

Chandler's monsoon season lasts from June 15 to September 30. Even mid-life roofs can take damage from high winds, especially if tiles were already cracked or loose.

After a big storm, walk around the house and look for tile pieces, then check ceilings over the next few days. If you find damage, our storm damage repair team can document and fix it. Small storm repairs on a mid-life roof are usually quick.

Over the next five to ten years, many Old Stone Ranch roofs will reach re-felt age. Knowing that now helps you budget. We can tell you what condition your underlayment is in and roughly when it may need replacement.

When that time comes, a tile underlayment replacement typically reuses your existing tile, which keeps the look consistent with the HOA's standards. Check with the Old Stone Ranch HOA before changing tile color or style.

Probably not yet. At 15–20 years old, most roofs need maintenance and small repairs. An inspection will confirm your roof's condition.

Felt under tile commonly lasts 20–25 years in Arizona, so many roofs here may reach that point within the next decade, starting with Phase 1 homes.

Yes, at this age. A mid-life inspection catches cracked tiles, worn sealant and clogged valleys while they are cheap to fix, and it gives you a realistic timeline for future underlayment work.

Leaves and debris can clog valleys and gutters and hold moisture against the roof. Keeping them clear, especially before monsoon season, helps.

We don't have the Old Stone Ranch HOA's specific rules. Most Arizona HOAs require approval for changes in roof color or material.
How often should I have my roof inspected?
Every year or two is reasonable at this age, plus a check after any major storm.

Yes. We replace broken tiles with matching ones and check the underlayment underneath while we're there.
How do I book an Old Stone Ranch roof check?
Dial 602-548-3770 any weekday from 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

Not every roof fails on schedule. Orientation, attic ventilation and how many tiles have cracked over the years all change how fast felt wears. That's why a roof inspection at this age is useful: it tells you whether you have years of life left or should start planning now.

sections.h2: What usually goes first on a 20-year-old roof
bullets: Sealant around pipe boots, vents and skylights
Underlayment in valleys, where water concentrates
Felt at the eaves, which gets the most direct sun
Flashing where the roof meets a wall or a second story
Tiles cracked by foot traffic from satellite or solar installs
sections.body: On homes of this era, leaks often start in a few predictable places.

sections.h2: Solar panels and other roof penetrations
sections.body:
Many Chandler homes from the mid-2000s have had solar, satellite dishes or new vents added since they were built. Each installation means holes in the roof and people walking on tile, which can crack pieces and disturb flashing.

If your home has had any add-ons, ask us to look closely at those areas. Planning a re-felt before installing solar also avoids paying to remove and reinstall panels a few years later.

Underlayment wears out faster when the attic below it runs hot. Blocked soffit vents, crushed insulation baffles or too few roof vents trap heat under the deck, and that heat bakes the felt from underneath while the sun bakes it from above.

During an inspection we look at how your attic breathes. Simple fixes, such as clearing vents or adding ventilation during a re-felt, can help the new underlayment last longer and may make upstairs rooms a little more comfortable in summer.

For a 20-year-old roof, a targeted repair is often enough: replacing broken tiles, resealing flashings and patching a worn valley.

If the underlayment is failing in several areas, a tile underlayment replacement that reuses your existing tile is the long-term fix. A full replacement is usually only needed if the deck is damaged or a lot of tile is broken.

sections.h2: Storms, HOA rules and next steps

Storm season officially runs from June 15 through September 30. After strong winds, check for broken tile and new ceiling stains, and call us for storm damage repair if you find any.

We don't have the Sienna Community Association's roofing rules, but most Arizona HOAs review changes to roof color or material. Check with the association before choosing new tile.

That variety means you can't judge your roof by a neighbor's. We inspect each system on your home, tile, foam and flat, and give you a separate assessment for each.
Spray foam roofs are lightweight and well insulated, but they depend on a protective top coating. Sunlight breaks that coating down over time, and once it's thin, UV starts eroding the foam.
bullets: Recoat on schedule, typically every several years depending on the coating
Repair blisters, punctures and bird damage promptly
Keep drains and scuppers clear so water doesn't pond
Look for exposed, crumbly foam, a sign the coating is gone

sections.body:
Flat sections over patios, courtyards and connecting rooms are common on larger custom homes. Rolled and hot-mop roofs can blister and crack in the heat, and seams where flat meets pitched tile are a frequent leak point.

We repair and replace flat roofs, and an elastomeric coating can extend the life of a sound flat roof. Our foam roofing services cover recoats and repairs.

The pitched portions of most Whitewing homes are tile. On homes from 2006 and later, the underlayment is between about 12 and 20 years old. Felt typically lasts 20–25 years in Arizona, so the oldest homes here are approaching that window.

For now, most tile roofs need inspection and targeted repairs. As they age, a tile underlayment replacement will reuse your existing tile and replace the felt beneath.

sections.h2: A roof that fits Agritopia's historic-style homes
sections.body:
Agritopia was planned around early-20th-century Arizona building styles. You'll see Spanish eclectic homes, American Craftsman designs, Northern European revival looks and ranch houses, sometimes on the same block. That variety is part of the charm, and it also means there isn't one standard roof here.

Tile is confirmed on at least one Phase 4 home from 2005, and tile is common across the East Valley. Beyond that, materials follow the architecture. When a roof on a home like this needs work, the aim is to keep the profile, color and edge details true to the house so the repair or replacement doesn't stand out from the street.

Before we quote any job, we look at the existing material, the pitch and how the roof meets walls, porches and chimneys. That tells us whether a tile roof, an asphalt shingle roof or a low-slope section is the right way to match what's already there.

sections.h2: What two decades of Arizona sun does to a 2003 roof
sections.body:
Ground was broken for homes in Agritopia in 2003, so the earliest roofs are now roughly 18–23 years old. Concrete and clay tile can outlast that by a wide margin, but the felt underlayment under the tile usually doesn't. In our climate, felt often lasts about 20–25 years before it dries out, cracks and stops shedding water.

Tile hides this kind of wear. A roof can look fine from the sidewalk while the layer underneath is brittle at the eaves, in the valleys and around vents. Often the first clue is a ceiling stain after a monsoon storm.

If yours is one of the earlier builds, a roof inspection shows where the underlayment stands before a leak reaches the inside. Some homes here have already had new roofs, so if you bought recently, check your disclosure paperwork for the roof's history.
bullets: Cracked or slipped tiles near the eaves and valleys
Brittle, crumbling felt visible at tile edges
Ceiling or wall stains after heavy rain
Loose or rusted flashing around vents and chimneys

sections.h2: Trees, gardens and gutters around the farm
sections.body:
Agritopia is built around a working organic farm, with a community garden, an orchard and mature landscaping along walkable streets. Shade is welcome in a Gilbert summer, but branches that hang over a roof drop leaves and fruit into valleys and gutters.

When debris piles up, rain backs up under the tile instead of running off. Branches that rub the roof in monsoon winds can crack tile too. A quick look at valleys and gutters in spring and again once storm season ends keeps small problems small. If you can't safely see your roof, we can check it for you.

sections.h2: HOA approval for roof work in Agritopia
sections.body:
Agritopia has a homeowners association, and its covenants shape how the neighborhood looks and feels. We haven't reviewed the association's specific roof rules, so check with the HOA before you change roof material or color. Repairs that match the existing roof usually raise fewer questions than a change of look.

For a replacement, get the HOA's requirements in writing early. We can supply the product names and color details an architectural request usually asks for, so paperwork doesn't hold up your project once it's ready to schedule.

sections.h2: Choosing between repair, re-felt and replacement
sections.body: Most aging roofs here will fall into one of three paths. Which one makes sense depends on the age of the underlayment, the condition of the roof covering and how long you plan to stay in the home. Every roof is different, so we don't quote prices without seeing it; our Roofing Cost Guide explains what drives the cost of each option, and financing is available if you ask during the estimate.
bullets: Repair: replacing broken tiles, resealing flashing or fixing one leak area on a roof that's otherwise sound
Underlayment replacement: lifting the tile, installing new underlayment and relaying the existing tile, swapping out any broken pieces
Full replacement: a complete new roof when the covering itself is worn out or you want a different material

sections.h2: A Gilbert roofer that's local to Agritopia
sections.body:
Our only office is in Gilbert, at 16308 E Fairview St, so Agritopia is part of our home town. We've been family owned and operated since 1993 and have completed more than 2,500 projects across the East Valley.

Can you match the look of my Craftsman or Spanish-style home?

Why does my tile roof leak if the tiles look fine?

Tile mostly shields the layer beneath it. The underlayment does the real waterproofing, and felt often wears out after about 20–25 years of Arizona heat. Once it cracks, water that slips past the tile can reach the roof deck.
Can trees from the orchard and gardens hurt my roof?

Leaves and fruit can clog valleys and gutters, and branches can scrape or crack tile in monsoon winds. Trimming branches back from the roofline and clearing debris once or twice a year helps prevent leaks.
When is the best time to have an Agritopia roof checked?
Spring is ideal, because there's time to fix problems before monsoon season starts on June 15. A second look after the season ends on September 30 can catch storm damage before winter rain.

sections.h2: Power Ranch from a roofer's point of view
sections.body:
Power Ranch is a large master-planned community in southeast Gilbert, developed by Sunbelt Holdings with DMB. It has clubhouses, an event pavilion, catch-and-release fishing lakes, a soccer complex and a trail system. Published size figures for the community differ from source to source, so we won't quote a home count, but it's big enough that roofs here span several builders and phases.

That matters for roofing. A home built in the first phases and one built years later can sit a few streets apart yet be at very different points in their roof life. The first question we ask in Power Ranch is simple: when was your home built, and has the roof been worked on since?

sections.h2: First-phase homes and the 20-year underlayment window
sections.body:
The Power Ranch Community Association was incorporated in October 2000, so the earliest homes likely date to around 2001–2002. On a concrete tile roof, the tile itself can last for decades, but the felt underlayment beneath it is often ready for replacement after about 20–25 years of Arizona heat.

For many first-phase homes, that window is open now. Waiting for a leak isn't the cheapest strategy, because by the time water shows up indoors it may already have soaked the roof deck. A roof inspection looks under the tile at the eaves, valleys and penetrations to see how much life is left.

When the underlayment is worn but the tile is sound, the usual fix is to lift the tile, install new underlayment and relay the same tile, replacing broken pieces as we go.

Richmond American is confirmed on a 2008 Power Ranch home with a tile roof, and Blandford Homes, D.R. Horton and Shea Homes are also named as builders here. Each builder chose its own tile profiles, colors, vent styles and flashing details, and those choices varied by phase.

For repairs, that means replacement tiles need to match your specific roof, not just the neighborhood in general. If you have spare tiles from the builder in your garage or side yard, keep them. They're often the closest match when a few pieces crack.

sections.h2: After a monsoon storm in southeast Gilbert
sections.body: Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30, and the strongest storms bring sudden wind gusts and heavy rain. On tile roofs, wind can lift or slide tiles at ridges and edges, and flying debris can crack them. Once the storm passes, check from the ground first and leave the climbing to us.
bullets: Tiles sitting crooked, missing or broken on the lawn
Ridge or hip caps that look shifted
Water stains on ceilings or around skylights
Torn coating or ponding water on flat patio sections

sections.body:
Many East Valley homes from this era pair a pitched tile roof with a flatter section over a patio or addition. Low-slope areas don't drain as quickly as tile, and their coatings break down faster in direct sun.

If your home has one, we can repair it or recoat it with an elastomeric coating or spray foam system, depending on what's there now. It's worth checking these areas whenever the main roof is inspected.

sections.h2: Working with the Power Ranch Community Association
sections.body:

We haven't reviewed the roof provisions, so read them or call the management company before changing tile color or style. Like-for-like repairs are usually simpler than a change in appearance.

If you live in Trilogy at Power Ranch, remember that it has its own HOA with its own rules, separate from the main Power Ranch association.

We're a family-owned roofing contractor based in Gilbert, licensed, bonded and insured under Arizona ROC #096629. To talk through a repair or replacement, call 602-548-3770, Monday to Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

If your home is from the early 2000s and the roof hasn't been redone, it's worth checking. Felt underlayment often lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, and many first-phase homes are in that range now.

We try to match profile and color as closely as possible. Matching is easier when you still have leftover tiles from the builder, so hang on to any you have.

The association's CC&Rs are posted on its website, and we haven't reviewed the roof provisions. Check with the HOA before changing color or style; we can provide product details for an approval request.

No. Trilogy at Power Ranch is a separate 55+ age-restricted community with its own HOA, so its owners should follow that association's rules.
What should I do after a monsoon storm damages my roof?

Look from the ground for displaced tiles and check ceilings for stains, then call us during business hours to arrange a look. If water is coming in, move belongings away and catch drips until we can get there.

Yes. We repair and recoat low-slope sections with elastomeric coatings or spray foam, and we can check them alongside your tile roof.

Phone is the only way to reach us: 602-548-3770, weekdays from 7 am to 5 pm. Our office is at 16308 E Fairview St in Gilbert.

facts.location: Power Ranch area of southeast Gilbert
facts.type: 55+ age-restricted active-adult community with its own HOA; private
facts.roofs: Tile on a 2002 Shea Homes listing

sections.body:
Trilogy at Power Ranch is an age-restricted active-adult community for residents 55 and older, built by Shea Homes under its Trilogy brand. It has its own HOA, separate from the larger Power Ranch community around it.

Roofing here isn't different in materials, but it often is in how people want to work. Many homeowners prefer clear written findings, photos of what we saw, and time to talk it over with family before deciding. We're glad to work that way.

sections.h2: Early-2000s tile roofs at the 20-year mark
sections.body:
A home in Trilogy Unit 4 built in 2002 shows a tile roof, which is typical of the community. At more than 20 years old, those roofs are entering the period when felt underlayment commonly wears out in Arizona.

The tile can still look good from the street. The trouble is underneath, where heat has dried the felt until it cracks. A roof inspection checks the eaves, valleys and areas around vents for brittle underlayment and gives you a clear picture before any leak appears.

Falls from ladders and roofs are a serious risk at any age, and tile is slippery and easy to break underfoot. There's no need to climb up to check after a storm. Look from the ground, check your ceilings and attic access, and let us do the climbing.
bullets: Look for tiles out of place from the yard or street
Check ceilings for new stains or bubbling paint
Listen for dripping in the attic or walls during rain
Note any debris on the roof you can see from the ground

sections.body:
A roof replacement or underlayment project is a big decision, and many Trilogy homeowners like to include adult children or a trusted friend. You're welcome to have someone join the walk-through or the estimate visit, in person or on speakerphone.

We'll explain the options in plain language: repair what's damaged, replace the underlayment and reuse your tile, or replace the roof entirely. We'll also tell you when a roof doesn't need work yet. Financing is available if you ask during the estimate.

sections.h2: Private community access and HOA review
sections.body:
Trilogy at Power Ranch is a private community. When you call to schedule, give us any entry instructions we'll need so our crew can arrive on time.

The Trilogy HOA is separate from Power Ranch, and we haven't reviewed its roof guidelines. Check with the association before changing tile color or style. Like-for-like repairs usually need less review than a new look.

sections.h2: Planning around summer travel and monsoon season
sections.body:
If you travel during the summer, schedule a roof check in spring before you leave. Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30, and a small leak in an empty home can do a lot of damage before anyone notices. Ask a neighbor or family member to check ceilings after big storms while you're away.

To book a visit, call 602-548-3770 weekdays between 7 am and 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

Homes date to the early 2000s, including a 2002 Shea home with a tile roof. That puts many roofs past 20 years.

If the roof is original, it's a good time to check. Felt underlayment commonly lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona. An inspection tells you how much life is left.
Can my son or daughter join the estimate?
Of course. Family members are welcome at the walk-through, in person or by phone, and we'll answer their questions as well as yours.
Should I check my roof myself after a storm?
Please don't climb up. Check from the ground and look for ceiling stains inside. If something looks wrong, call us and we'll take a look.
How do I get your crew into the community?
Share your entry instructions when you phone to book, and our crew will use them on the day of the visit.
Do I need HOA approval for roof work in Trilogy?
Check with the Trilogy HOA before changing tile color or style. We haven't reviewed its rules, but we can provide product details for your request.
What should I do before leaving for the summer?
Have the roof checked in spring, ideally before monsoon season starts on June 15, and ask someone to look at ceilings after big storms while you're gone.

facts.builders: KB Home; Lennar also listed by one real estate source
facts.type: Master-planned community with lakes and HOA

sections.body:
Layton Lakes was developed over roughly a decade, with listings showing homes from the mid-2010s and a KB Home section that opened in January 2020. A 2020 KB Home in the community shows a tile roof.

A tile roof this young usually still has plenty of life in its underlayment, which often lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona. That shifts the focus to protecting what you have: fixing storm damage quickly, keeping valleys clear, and making sure anything mounted on the roof was sealed properly.

sections.h2: After a monsoon: what to look for
sections.body: Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30, and storms can push wind gusts strong enough to lift or crack tiles, even on a new roof. Most storm damage is easy to repair if it's caught early.
bullets: Broken tile pieces in the yard or on the driveway
Ridge caps or edge tiles that look shifted
Debris such as branches or patio furniture on the roof
New ceiling stains or damp spots in the garage

sections.body:
If you bought from KB Home or another builder, find your closing documents and read what they say about roof coverage. Builder workmanship warranties and tile manufacturer warranties are separate, and each has its own terms and time limits.

Before you have any roof work done on a newer home, it helps to know what's still covered. If a problem falls outside that coverage, or the coverage has ended, we can make the repair.

sections.h2: Solar, satellite dishes and roof penetrations
sections.body:
On newer homes, a common source of leaks isn't the roof itself but what's been added to it. Every bolt for a solar rack, satellite dish or vent is a hole through the underlayment, and if it isn't flashed and sealed correctly, water follows it in.

If you've added equipment to your roof and notice a stain nearby, call us. We can reseal the penetration, replace cracked tiles around it and check the underlayment underneath.

sections.h2: When Layton Lakes roofs will need underlayment work
sections.body:
Based on typical felt lifespans, homes built in the mid-2010s may start needing underlayment work in the 2030s, and 2020 homes after that. Heat, sun exposure and how well the roof is maintained all affect the timing.

An occasional roof inspection as your home ages gives you a baseline and helps you plan instead of being surprised.

The Layton Lakes Community Association oversees the community, and sections such as Signatures at Layton Lakes are part of it. We haven't reviewed its roof guidelines, so ask the association before changing roof materials or colors.

We're a family-owned Gilbert roofing company, licensed under ROC #096629. The number is 602-548-3770, and we pick up weekdays from 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

Probably not yet. Tile roofs from the 2010s and 2020 are usually still within their normal service life. Repairs and maintenance are more common needs at this stage.
Can a newer roof be damaged in a monsoon?
Yes. Strong gusts can lift or crack tiles on any roof, regardless of age. Check from the ground after big storms and call if you see something out of place.
Should I check my builder warranty before calling a roofer?
It's a good idea. Look at your closing documents for roof coverage terms and time limits. If the issue isn't covered, we can make the repair.
My solar panels were installed and now I have a leak. Can you help?
Yes. Leaks around solar mounts usually come from penetrations that weren't flashed or sealed well. We can reseal them and replace any cracked tiles around them.
When will Layton Lakes roofs need new underlayment?
Felt underlayment usually lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, so mid-2010s homes may need work sometime in the 2030s. Exact timing varies by roof.

Like-for-like repairs usually raise few issues, but check with the Layton Lakes Community Association before changing roof materials or colors.

Ring our Gilbert office at 602-548-3770 between 7 am and 5 pm on a weekday.

Homes from the first phases, around 2005, are reaching 20 years. Felt underlayment under tile commonly lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, so these roofs are entering the stretch where it starts to dry out and crack.

Getting an inspection now lets you plan the work on your schedule. If the tile is in good shape, replacing the underlayment and relaying the existing tile is usually the most practical fix.

sections.h2: Later phases: keeping a younger roof healthy
sections.body:
Homes from 2010–2015 still have years before underlayment typically becomes an issue. For these roofs, the priorities are simple: replace broken tiles quickly, keep valleys and gutters clear, and check flashing around vents and walls.

Cracked tiles are easy to overlook but let heat and water reach the underlayment early. Fixing them keeps the whole roof on track to last as long as it should.

sections.h2: Common tile roof problems we see in the East Valley
sections.body: Across Gilbert, tile roofs from the 2000s and 2010s tend to develop the same handful of issues. Most are inexpensive to fix when caught early.
bullets: Tiles cracked by foot traffic from other trades
Debris build-up in valleys that slows drainage
Dried-out sealant at pipe and vent flashings
Bird nests under the edge tiles at the eaves
Wind-shifted ridge caps after monsoon storms

The Lyon's Gate HOA is managed by Brown Community Management. We haven't reviewed its roof guidelines, so contact the association before changing roof color or materials. Matching repairs are generally the least complicated.

faqs: Is it Lyons Gate or Lyon's Gate?
The official spelling is Lyon's Gate, named for William Lyon Homes. Both spellings refer to the same community at Higley Rd and Ray Rd.
When were Lyons Gate homes built?
Homes were built from about 2005 to 2015, so roof ages vary by phase.
Do Lyons Gate homes have tile roofs?
A 2011 William Lyon home shows a tile roof. We confirm the material on each home during a visit.
My Lyons Gate home was built in 2005. Does it need new underlayment?
It may soon. Felt underlayment commonly lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, and 2005 homes are entering that range. An inspection will show its condition.
What does underlayment replacement involve?
We remove the tile, take off the old underlayment, install new underlayment and flashing, and then relay the tile, replacing any broken pieces.
Who manages the Lyon's Gate HOA?
Brown Community Management manages it. Check with them about roof guidelines before changing materials or colors.
Can cracked tiles really cause a leak?
Yes, over time. A cracked tile exposes the underlayment to sun and water, which wears it out faster and can eventually let water into the home.
How do I schedule a roof estimate in Lyons Gate?
Dial 602-548-3770 during weekday office hours, 7 am to 5 pm, and ask about financing when we visit.
Why do bird nests matter on a tile roof?
Birds sometimes build under open edge tiles at the eaves. Nesting material can trap water and block drainage, and the birds can loosen tiles. Bird stops installed along the eaves help keep them out.
Do homes on the east and west sides of Higley Rd need different roof care?
Not because of which side they're on. What matters more is the home's build year and phase, since Lyon's Gate was built over about 10 years.

sections.h2: Old and new under one name
sections.body:
Cooley Station is a village-style, mixed-use community with tree-lined streets and green space. Building started years ago and hasn't stopped: listings show a 2006 Phase 2 home by Capital Pacific Homes and new Fulton Homes construction in 2026.

Both use tile roofs, but they're at opposite ends of their lives. A roofer who treats every Cooley Station home the same isn't paying attention, so we start by asking when your home was built.

The earliest homes are about 20 years old now. Concrete tile holds up well, but felt underlayment beneath it typically lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, and the hottest, most exposed slopes often wear out first.

If your home is from the early phases and the roof has never been worked on, an inspection is the best next step. We'll check the underlayment at the eaves and valleys and tell you whether a repair, a lift-and-relay or a replacement fits the roof's condition.

sections.h2: Just moved into a new build?
sections.body:
If you bought one of the newer homes, your roof should be in great shape. Still, it's worth knowing what your builder's warranty covers and for how long. Keep your closing paperwork handy and report any roof concerns to the builder while coverage applies.

After coverage ends, or for damage that isn't covered, such as storm damage or tiles cracked by other trades, we can handle the repair.

sections.h2: Concrete tile: strengths and weak spots
sections.body: Concrete tile is common across Gilbert because it handles heat and sun well and lasts a long time. But it has weaknesses worth knowing:
bullets: It can crack if someone walks on it the wrong way
Wind can shift edge and ridge tiles during monsoon storms
It hides worn underlayment, so leaks seem to appear suddenly
Flashing and sealant around penetrations age faster than the tile

sections.body:
Some Cooley Station homes may have a flatter roof over a patio, casita or addition. Water moves off a low-slope surface more slowly than off pitched tile, and the sun wears down its protective coating year after year.

We repair and recoat these areas with elastomeric coatings or spray foam, and we can look them over whenever we check the main roof.

Cooley Station has more than one homeowners association, including the Cooley Station HOA and the Cooley Station North Community Association. Find out which one your home belongs to before planning a roof change. We haven't reviewed their roof rules, but matching repairs are usually the simplest to approve.

sections.h2: Monsoon prep and how to reach us
sections.body:
Monsoon season runs June 15–September 30. Before it starts, clear debris from valleys, replace any cracked tiles and check flat patio sections for worn coating. After big storms, look from the ground and call if something looks off.

We're a family-owned roofing contractor in Gilbert, licensed under ROC #096629. Dial 602-548-3770 Monday through Friday, 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

faqs: When were Cooley Station homes built?
Listings show homes from 2006 through new construction in 2026, and the community is still building.
Who built homes in Cooley Station?
Capital Pacific Homes built in the early phases, and Fulton Homes is building newer sections.
What kind of roofs are in Cooley Station?
Listings from both 2006 and 2026 show tile roofs, including concrete tile.
Does my 2006 Cooley Station roof need new underlayment?
It may be time to check. Felt underlayment commonly lasts about 20–25 years in Arizona, and early homes are reaching that range.
My new Cooley Station home has a roof leak. What should I do?
Contact your builder first if the home is still under warranty. If coverage has ended or the issue isn't covered, call us for a repair.
Can workers from other trades damage my tile roof?
Yes. Solar, HVAC and satellite installers can crack tiles by walking on them. If someone has been on your roof, it's worth a check.
Which HOA covers my Cooley Station home?
Cooley Station includes the Cooley Station HOA and the Cooley Station North Community Association. Check your closing documents or ask your management company.
Do you repair flat roofs on Cooley Station homes?
Yes. We repair and recoat flat and low-slope sections using elastomeric coatings or spray foam.
How do I contact you about a Cooley Station roof?
We answer 602-548-3770 Monday through Friday, 7 am to 5 pm, and the office is closed on weekends.
Why do concrete tile leaks seem to start suddenly?
The tile hides the underlayment, so wear builds up out of sight for years. When the underlayment finally cracks through, the first sign is often a stain that shows up after one heavy storm.

facts.type: Subdivision within the Morrison Ranch master plan with its own HOA

sections.body:
Higley Groves sits in the northern part of Morrison Ranch, north of Elliot Rd. Shea Homes and Trend Homes built its homes around 2000–2001, and Greystone built in the neighboring Higley Groves West. These are among the first homes in all of Morrison Ranch.

The streets are tree-lined and tied into the Morrison Ranch greenbelt system. The roofs, though, have now seen about a quarter-century of Arizona summers, and that's the main thing driving roofing decisions here.

Tile roofs from 2000–2001 are past the 20–25 years that felt underlayment usually lasts in our heat. The tile on top may still be fine, but the waterproof layer beneath it has likely become brittle, especially at the eaves and in the valleys where water concentrates.

That's why homes in Higley Groves are strong candidates for underlayment replacement. Waiting for a leak can mean paying for drywall and decking repairs on top of the roof work. A roof inspection shows exactly how worn the underlayment is.

When the tile is still sound, we can usually keep it. Here's what the process looks like on a typical Higley Groves home:

  1. We remove the tile carefully and stack it on the roof or nearby.
  2. We strip the old underlayment down to the deck and check the decking.
  3. We replace any soft or damaged decking.
  4. We install new underlayment, battens where needed and new flashing.
  5. We relay your original tile, replacing broken pieces with the closest match.

The result looks like your original roof but has a fresh waterproof layer underneath. If too much tile is damaged or worn, a full replacement may be the better option.

sections.h2: Higley Groves vs. Higley Groves West
sections.body:
The Town of Gilbert lists Higley Groves at Morrison Ranch and Higley Groves West as separate associations. Higley Groves has its own HOA, and homes may also fall under the Morrison Ranch master association. Before changing your roof's look, confirm which associations apply to you and what each requires.

We haven't reviewed their roof rules, but a lift-and-relay that reuses your existing tile usually keeps the appearance unchanged, which tends to make approval simple.

sections.h2: If your roof was already replaced
sections.body: Some homes in Higley Groves already have new roofs; at least one listing notes it. If yours was redone, ask the previous owner or check your paperwork for when and what was done. A newer roof here needs the same care as any other: replace cracked tiles, keep valleys clear and check flashing after big storms.

We're family owned and operated, based in Gilbert since our founding in 1993, and licensed under ROC #096629. Our office phone, 602-548-3770, is staffed weekdays from 7 am to 5 pm. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.

sections.h2: What happens to underlayment after two decades
sections.body:
Tile sheds most rain, but some water always gets underneath. The underlayment is what carries that water off the roof. After years of attic-level heat, the felt dries out, shrinks and cracks, especially at the laps and around nails.

Once that happens, water that slips past the tile can reach the wood deck. You may see it as a ceiling stain, but it often starts as hidden rot that only shows up later. Catching it early usually keeps the fix simpler.

sections.h2: How a tile roof actually keeps water out
sections.body:
Many homeowners assume the tile is the waterproof layer. It is really the first line of defense. Tile sheds most rain and shields what is beneath it from the sun, but wind-driven rain still gets underneath, and the underlayment carries that water down and off the roof.

When the underlayment dries out and cracks, water that gets past the tile can reach the deck and eventually the ceiling. That is why a roof can look fine from the street and still leak.

sections.h2: Early clues your underlayment is wearing out
sections.body: You can catch many problems before they cause interior damage. Watch for:
bullets: Leaks that appear only in heavy or wind-driven rain
Dark, flaky bits of felt in gutters or on walkways
Tiles that have slid down or out of line
Water marks on the attic deck or insulation
A previous patch that keeps leaking nearby

sections.h2: The fix: lift, re-felt and relay
sections.body:
An underlayment replacement is the standard repair for a tile roof whose felt is worn out. We remove the tile, take off the old underlayment, repair any damaged decking, install new underlayment and flashing, and put the tile back. Cracked tiles are replaced with a matching product when one is available.

It is a bigger job than a spot repair but far less than replacing everything. If you want to compare approaches, our tile roofs and roof replacement pages explain the differences.

sections.h2: How a lift and relay works
sections.body:
A lift and relay is the most common fix for a tile roof of this age. Here's what happens, step by step:

  1. We remove the tiles and stack them safely on the roof or in the yard.
  2. We tear off the old underlayment and check the wood deck for damage.
  3. We install new underlayment, plus new flashing and vent jacks where needed.
  4. We reset the tiles, swapping in replacements for any that are cracked.

The result is essentially a new waterproofing system under your existing tile. Learn more on our tile roofs page.

Descriptions of Gilbert Ranch mention some townhomes alongside the single-family houses. If you share a roof line with a neighbor, your roof connects to theirs, and water doesn't respect property lines. Before re-roofing, find out from your HOA documents who is responsible for which part.

When neighbors re-roof at the same time, the seam between units can be handled as one continuous job, which is cleaner than tying new underlayment into old. It's worth a conversation over the fence before you schedule.

Listings show Wind Drift homes built in 1990 and 1995, including Hunters Point at Wind Drift, with tile roofs. A roof from those years has been through more than 30 Arizona summers. Unless it's been redone, the original felt underlayment is well beyond the 20–25 years it typically lasts.

On roofs this old, we often find underlayment that has turned brittle or worn through along the eaves and valleys, flashing that has rusted or pulled away, and ridge mortar that is cracking. Any one of those can let water in during a monsoon downpour.

Because Wind Drift is older, some homes have already been re-roofed once. If you bought here, you may not know whether the roof is original or a later replacement. Seller disclosures, permits and receipts can help, and so can an inspection.

If your roof was redone in the 2000s, it may be nearing its own underlayment replacement. The real age of your roof, not just the house, is what matters.

Wind Drift is a master HOA community with sub-neighborhoods and a mix of single-family homes and townhomes. In townhome sections, roofs are often connected, and responsibility for them varies. Some associations handle roofs; others leave them to owners. Check your sub-association's documents before you plan work.

If you're responsible for your own roof but share a roof line, talk with your neighbors. Re-roofing adjoining units together can make the joint between them cleaner and more watertight.

sections.h2: Re-felt vs. full replacement on an older home
sections.body: On a 30-year-old tile roof, both options are on the table. Read more about roof replacement and our tile roof services. These factors usually decide which makes more sense:
bullets: How many tiles are cracked, brittle or no longer available to match
Whether the wood deck has soft spots or water damage
Whether you want to change the look of your roof
How long you plan to stay in the home
What your HOA allows for tile color and style

sections.body:
Wind Drift has a community lake and sits close to Downtown Gilbert and Freestone Park. Three decades of growth means plenty of mature trees in the neighborhood. They provide welcome shade but drop leaves into valleys and gutters and can scrape tiles in the wind.

Keeping branches trimmed and valleys clear is a cheap way to protect an older roof. It also makes the roof easier to inspect.

If it's the original roof, the underlayment is very likely past its typical 20–25 year life. The tiles may still be good, which is why a re-felt is often an option.

Not usually. We replace only the damaged decking we find once the old underlayment is off, and we'll show you what we found.

If your roof is original and showing wear, getting it done before June 15 is a good plan. Storms are often when weak underlayment starts to leak.

It can. Ask about financing during your estimate and we'll walk you through it.

sections.body:
Gilbert grew up around a rail line. In 1902, William "Bobby" Gilbert provided land to the Arizona Eastern Railway for a route between Phoenix and Florence, and the town that formed there was incorporated on July 6, 1920. For years it was a farming town known as the hay shipping capital of the world.

Today the Heritage District is the heart of Downtown Gilbert. As late as 1980 the town had fewer than 6,000 residents, so the neighborhoods closest to downtown hold some of Gilbert's oldest homes alongside much newer ones.

Layered roofs add weight and hide problems in the deck, so a re-roof on an older home usually means tearing off down to the wood and fixing any damage. Our sloped roofs and flat roofing pages explain the options for each roof shape.

Several new homes have gone up near downtown in the last few years, including listings from 2022 and 2023. Roofs on these homes are just starting their service life. The main jobs for now are checking for installation issues, replacing any tiles or shingles damaged by storms, and watching the flashing where roof planes meet walls.
